levels.title: The Three Colored Hats Enigma
levels.prompt: Three logicians (A, B, C) stand in single file facing a wall: C sees B and A; B sees only A; A sees no one. A referee shows 3 white hats and 2 black hats, then places one hat on each person. C is asked if he knows his hat color and says 'No'. B hears this, is asked, and also says 'No'. Hearing both, A confidently announces his hat color. What color is A's hat?
options: Indeterminate without knowing C's hat color
Neither; the game is an impossible paradox
levels.hint: If C saw two black hats ahead of him, what would he immediately announce? Since C said 'No', B knows that A and B cannot BOTH be black.
levels.explanation: If A and B both had black hats, C would have instantly known his own was white. Because C said 'No', B knows that at least one of (A, B) is white. If A had a black hat, B would immediately know B has white. Because B also said 'No', A cannot have a black hat. Thus, A's hat is WHITE!

levels.title: The Fox, Goose, and Grain Crossing
levels.prompt: A farmer must transport a fox, a goose, and a bag of grain across a river in a boat that can only carry himself and ONE item. If left alone without the farmer, the fox eats the goose, or the goose eats the grain. What is the minimum number of one-way boat trips required to bring all three safely across?
levels.hint: You may bring an item BACK across the river to prevent an illegal pairing.
levels.explanation: Trip 1: Take Goose across (Fox & Grain safe). Trip 2: Return alone. Trip 3: Take Fox across. Trip 4: Bring Goose BACK. Trip 5: Take Grain across. Trip 6: Return alone. Trip 7: Take Goose across. Total = 7 trips!

levels.title: Hilbert's Infinite Hotel Expansion
levels.prompt: Hilbert's Grand Hotel contains countably infinite rooms (numbered 1, 2, 3, ...), and every single room is currently occupied. A new infinite bus containing countably infinite new guests arrives. How can the night manager accommodate all infinite new guests without evicting any current guest?
options: Move each current guest in room n to room 2n, freeing all infinite odd-numbered rooms (1, 3, 5, ...) for the new arrivals
Add one extra floor onto the infinite skyscraper
Ask each guest to share their room with one new visitor
It is impossible because infinity cannot hold another infinity
levels.hint: Consider the parity of positive integers: even numbers vs odd numbers.
levels.explanation: By shifting each existing guest from room n to room 2n, all existing guests occupy even rooms (2, 4, 6, ...). This leaves every odd-numbered room (1, 3, 5, ...) completely empty—providing countably infinite rooms for the infinite new arrivals!

levels.title: The Pirate Gold Distribution
levels.prompt: 5 rational, ruthless pirates (ranked 1 to 5, where 1 is senior captain) must divide 100 gold coins. The senior pirate proposes a distribution. All pirates vote (including proposer). If at least 50% approve, the plan passes. Otherwise, the proposer is thrown to sharks and the next senior pirate proposes. Every pirate wants to survive, maximize gold, and prefers throwing others to sharks if payoffs are equal. What does Pirate 1 propose?
options: Pirate 1 keeps 98 coins, gives 0 to Pirate 2, 1 to Pirate 3, 0 to Pirate 4, and 1 to Pirate 5
Pirate 1 divides 20 coins equally to all 5 pirates
Pirate 1 keeps 50 coins and gives 50 coins to Pirate 2
Pirate 1 keeps 97 coins, gives 1 to Pirate 2, 1 to Pirate 3, and 1 to Pirate 4
levels.hint: Solve backwards from 2 pirates (P4 proposes 100 to self, 0 to P5). Then 3 pirates (P3 offers 1 to P5). Then 4 pirates, then 5.
levels.explanation: Using backward induction: With 2 pirates, P4 takes (100, 0). With 3 pirates, P3 needs 1 vote, buys P5 with 1 coin: (99, 0, 1). With 4 pirates, P2 buys P4 with 1 coin: (99, 0, 1, 0). With 5 pirates, P1 needs 2 other votes; he offers 1 coin to P3 and 1 coin to P5 (who would receive 0 under P2): (98, 0, 1, 0, 1)!

levels.title: The Three Cards in the Box
levels.prompt: A box contains three cards: Card A is black on both sides; Card B is white on both sides; Card C is black on one side and white on the other. You draw a random card and place it on a table without looking at the bottom. The visible top face is BLACK. What is the probability that the bottom face is ALSO black?
levels.hint: Count individual black FACES, not whole cards. How many black faces exist in the box?
levels.explanation: Bertrand's Box Paradox: There are 3 black faces in total across the cards (Face 1 of A, Face 2 of A, Face 1 of C). Since you see a black face, you are looking at one of these three equally likely faces. In 2 of those 3 cases (Face 1 or 2 of Card A), the other side is black. Therefore, probability is 2/3!
